summary: Marswalk Mission Planner is a layered 3D map of Jezero crater, the Perseverance landing site, for the first astronauts who will walk there. It computes on NASA data to answer the crew's real question: can I get there, do the science, and get home alive? It fuses eight NASA and USGS datasets (HiRISE terrain and imagery, CRISM minerals, THEMIS thermal, the USGS geologic map, MEDA weather, MSL RAD radiation, DONKI space weather, Perseverance's traverse and photos) to plan routes priced in kilograms of oxygen and watt-hours of battery. It shows the area the astronaut can still return from shrinking as the EVA clock runs, flags radio dead zones and distance from shelter for solar storms, and replans live when a dust storm, suit leak or solar alert hits. A machine-learning search finds more ground like the best science site, and a helmet HUD guides the walk. Every safety number traces to NASA data and tested code; our routes match Perseverance's real drive within about 100 m.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Marswalk Mission Planner is a 3D map and planning tool for a suited astronaut on a Marswalk at Jezero crater, the Perseverance landing site. It answers one question: can I get there, do the science, and get home alive?

A Python pipeline downloads eight public NASA and USGS datasets and aligns them on one 2-metre grid of about 3 million cells:

  • HiRISE terrain and imagery
  • CRISM minerals
  • THEMIS thermal
  • the USGS geologic map of Jezero
  • MEDA weather
  • MSL RAD radiation
  • NASA DONKI space weather
  • Perseverance's traverse and photos

On that data the tool:

  • Plans routes priced in life support. Every step costs time, oxygen (kg) and battery (Wh), using a published model of walking energy on slopes, scaled for Mars gravity and a pressurised suit. It offers three routes: safest, fastest and most science.
    • Radio dead zones, from a line-of-sight model that includes Mars curvature.
    • Radiation dose.
    • Solar storms predicted to reach Mars.
    • Worst-case time to reach shelter.
  • Replans live. When a dust storm, suit leak or solar particle alert hits, it replans from the current position with the oxygen and battery left.
  • Supports rover trips. It follows the Apollo walk-back rule: never drive farther than you could walk home.
    • A helmet heads-up display.
    • Perseverance's own photos of each stop.
    • A printable Curiosity-style mission map.
    • An Apollo-style cuff checklist.
    • An AI Flight Controller (Claude) whose every number is checked by code.

What benefits does it have?

  • It gives a decision, not just a picture: go, go by rover, or don't go, with the reason. Example: the 4-hour walk to Wildcat Ridge has radio contact on only 14% of the route and is up to 67 minutes from shelter. The same trip by rover takes 70 minutes and is safe.
    • Our planned route stays within 106 m on average of where Perseverance actually drove.
    • The ML was tested on half of the site it never saw.
    • 48 automated tests pass.
    • Every number traces to a NASA dataset.
  • Every assumption, such as suit mass, reserves and slope limits, is editable and sourced, so planners can test "what if".

What is the intended impact of the project?

To help future crews and mission planners plan Mars surface exploration that is both safe and scientifically productive: more science per walk, fewer risks discovered too late. The pipeline works for any Mars site with a HiRISE terrain model, so it could support landing-site studies and future EVA planning. It also shows how AI can assist astronauts without ever being trusted with a life-critical number.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Python: GDAL/rasterio and pyogrio (geospatial data), numpy, scipy, numba (fast route search), scikit-learn (machine learning), FastAPI (planner API).
  • Web: Vite, CesiumJS (3D Mars globe), uPlot (charts).
  • AI: the Anthropic Claude API with tool use.
  • Testing and hosting: pytest, Playwright, GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: a standard laptop; no special hardware.

How is your project creative?

  • It prices a map in oxygen instead of distance.
  • The shrinking "can I still get home" area is animated live on the graphics card.
  • Machine learning proposes science sites while physics decides whether they're safe.
  • One plan powers a 3D view, a helmet HUD, a printable mission map and a cuff checklist.
  • We check our own routes against where Perseverance really drove.

What factors did I consider?

  • Astronaut safety first: oxygen and battery reserves, the walk-back rule, radio contact, radiation, shelter time.
  • Honest data: only real NASA and USGS products, with limits stated openly.
  • AI safety: the language model never produces a safety-critical number; code verifies them all.
  • Validation: tests, route cases, the rover comparison, and ML checked against an independent geologic map.
  • Usability: one clear 3D view, a colour-blind-checked palette, a mobile layout, printable outputs, and a live demo anyone can open at https://9irija.github.io/marshalll_NASA/.
